uses: Cinnamon bark has a long history in the traditional medicine of China, India and Persia, where it was given for coughs, nerve pain and inflammation. In European tradition it was a warming spice for the stomach: Grieve and Culpeper used it to settle wind and nausea and to sweeten the breath, and it was often added to other remedies to improve their taste. The EMA recognizes it as a traditional remedy for mild bloating, wind and cramping, and for mild diarrhea. In Chinese practice it is combined with other herbs for colds. Most of all it is a kitchen spice, in baking and in spiced wines.
energetics: Culpeper called cinnamon hot and dry in the second degree
caution_pregnancy: Food amounts appear safe in pregnancy, but larger amounts of Ceylon cinnamon are considered unsafe, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal cinnamon in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Little is known about larger amounts of either Ceylon or cassia while breastfeeding; avoid.
caution_medications: No interaction with diabetes medicines is proven, but cinnamon may lower blood sugar (the evidence is mixed), so as a precaution ask your prescriber if you take them and watch for lows; in animals it raised levels of the diabetes drug pioglitazone. Case reports link cinnamon taken with a statin to hepatitis. Lab studies suggest it may affect liver enzymes that break down many drugs, and in theory some of its compounds could interact with a cancer medicine or with nicotine; whether any of this matters in people isn't known. Talk to your provider before using it if you take any medicine.
caution_conditions: Know which kind you have. Most cinnamon sold in North America is cassia (Cinnamomum aromaticum), which contains coumarin, a compound linked to liver problems. Ordinary cooking amounts usually don't supply enough coumarin to matter, but some cassia products are high in it, and heavy or long-term use of cassia could be a problem for sensitive people, such as anyone with liver disease. Ceylon cinnamon may hold only a trace. Larger amounts or long use can upset the stomach or cause allergic reactions. Don't use it if you are allergic to cinnamon or Peru balsam. Never swallow dry cinnamon powder as a dare; serious harm is possible. Use isn't established for anyone under 18.
caution_duration: If digestive complaints last more than 2 weeks, or diarrhea more than 2 days, see a doctor or qualified practitioner. With diarrhea, drink fluids first, and get help for bloody or repeated bouts.
caution_topical: Cinnamon oil or powder on the skin can cause irritation or allergic contact dermatitis. Herbal toothpaste and chewing gum with cinnamon have been linked to inflamed gums and mouth sores.
garden_harvest_timing: The spice is the dried inner bark of young shoots.
garden_water: A tropical tree that needs constant rain, heat and an even temperature
notes: An evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka, growing 20 to 30 feet tall, best in sandy soil in a sheltered spot; it isn't a plant for temperate gardens. Grieve records that the Dutch held the trade in wild cinnamon and opposed growing it, so it wasn't cultivated until 1776. Cassia, a relative Grieve thought inferior, is often sold in its place. Culpeper gives cinnamon no planet.
